201:
"And among them are those who say, 'Our Lord, give us good in this world and good in the Hereafter and protect us from the punishment of the Fire.'"

This is the du'a that answers the thin prayer of the previous verse. Not only dunya, and not a spirituality that pretends the world is nothing. Hasanah in this world — good that includes health, lawful provision, family, safety, useful knowledge — and hasanah in the Hereafter — Paradise, acceptance, company of the righteous — and protection from the Fire. Three requests that hold a whole religion of hope.

The Prophet, peace be upon him, used this du'a more than any other, as Aishah reported. He taught it as the balanced tongue of a believer who neither worships the world nor pretends he does not live in it. Good in dunya is asked from Allah so it does not have to be begged from sin; good in akhirah is asked so success never ends at a funeral; protection from the Fire keeps fear healthy without despair.

After hajj rites, after any worship, this is a complete way to speak. If your old prayers were only for salary, expand them. If they were only for deathbed safety while you neglected the means of a decent life, expand them the other way. Our Lord, both goods — and save us from the Fire.

Whether you are on the plain or reading from far away, the point is the same: rites without taqwa are tourism, and taqwa without remembrance fades. Ask for a hajj mabrur or for a heart that walks as if it had stood at Arafat.
202:
"Those will have a share of what they have earned, and Allah is swift in account."

The people of the balanced du'a in the previous verse are not left with poetry alone. They have a nasib — a share — from what they earned. Du'a opens the door; earning walks through it. The Quran refuses both the laziness that only asks and the arrogance that only works without asking. Hasanah in both worlds is requested, then kasab is named as the path of the share.

Allah is sari' al-hisab — swift in reckoning. Swift does not mean careless. It means no backlog can hide a deed, no queue can delay justice forever, and the account is not too complex for Him. The Prophet, peace be upon him, said people will be judged with ease or with scrutiny, and that none is saved by his deeds alone but by Allah's mercy — yet deeds remain the evidence of what the servant was aiming for. He also said "be in this world as a stranger or a traveller," so that earning for the akhirah stays urgent.

Hold the two truths together: your share is tied to what you earn, and the Accountant is fast. That combination makes procrastination look less clever. Scatter good in both worlds while the market of days is open, and let the speed of His hisab speed up your repentance and your charity.

203:
"And remember Allah during numbered days. Then whoever hastens in two days — there is no sin upon him; and whoever delays — there is no sin upon him — for him who fears Allah. And fear Allah and know that you will be gathered to Him."

The ayyam ma'dudat are the days of tashriq after the sacrifice, filled with takbir and the remaining rites of Mina. Dhikr is the occupation of the days, not empty waiting for departure. Then flexibility: leaving Mina in two days is allowed, staying longer is allowed — for the one who has taqwa. The concession is not a toy for the heedless; it is ease for the God-fearing who still order their hajj by fear of Allah rather than by whim.

The Prophet, peace be upon him, stayed and also permitted hastening, and he said the days of tashriq are days of eating, drinking, and remembrance of Allah. Fear Allah and know you will be gathered to Him — the hajj ends in a return to ordinary life, but the gathering ahead is not ordinary. Leave Mina when your taqwa allows; do not leave the remembrance when the plane takes off.

204:
"And of the people is he whose speech about worldly life amazes you, and he calls Allah to witness as to what is in his heart, yet he is the fiercest of opponents."

A portrait of a type every community meets. His worldly talk is polished — fluent on trade, politics, welfare of the city — and it impresses. He swears by Allah that his heart is sincere. Then the reality: he is aladd al-khisam — the most violent of adversaries when the truth costs him, when the court case turns, when the private interest is touched.

The Prophet, peace be upon him, warned that the most hated men to Allah include the quarrelsome one who argues without truth, and he said the signs of the hypocrite include lying, promise-breaking, and betrayal when trusted. Eloquence is not iman. Public oath is not inner light.

Test people by how they fight when crossed, not only by how they speak when the room applauds. And test yourself the same way. Amazing speech with a hostile core is a known disease; this verse diagnosed it early so the ummah would not appoint it to leadership on charm alone.

Leave the labels that make riba sound clever — 'growth product,' 'convenience fee,' 'time value' dressed to hide excess. The Quran already knew the arguments and still drew the line. Your task is exit with tawbah and principal, not a better brand name for the same war.
205:
"And when he goes away, he strives throughout the land to cause corruption therein and destroy crops and animals. And Allah does not like corruption."

When the impressive speaker leaves the gathering, his energy goes into fasad — corruption in the land — wrecking crops and livestock, the bases of people's survival. The image is agricultural and still modern: destroying livelihoods, poisoning wells of trust, burning fields of social peace for personal win. Allah does not love fasad. Love and hate here are legislative and real; what He does not love cannot be rebranded as necessary politics forever.

The Prophet, peace be upon him, forbade wanton destruction even in war — trees, animals, places of worship in various commands — and he said there is a reward in every living thing with a wet liver you treat kindly. Corruption that starves people while speeches feed egos is the opposite of his way.

Watch what people do after the microphone. The verse's villain is not quiet. He works hard — sa'a — at ruin. Hard work is not a virtue when the project is fasad. Allah's dislike of corruption is enough reason to refuse it even when it is efficient.

206:
"And when it is said to him, 'Fear Allah,' pride in the sin takes hold of him. Sufficient for him is Hell, and how wretched is the resting place."

The simplest advice becomes the trigger. Fear Allah — and pride, al-izzah bi al-ithm, seizes him, honour wrapped around the sin itself. He is too proud to be corrected. The more the reminder is true, the more his ego tightens. Hell is enough for him; bi's al-mihad — what a wretched bed.

The Prophet, peace be upon him, said the one who has a speck of pride in his heart will not enter Paradise, and he defined blameworthy kibr as rejecting truth and looking down on people. He accepted correction from companions and from a woman in the mosque. Pride that refuses "fear Allah" is refusing the ticket out of the sin.

If being reminded makes you cruel, this verse is a mirror. If you remind others, leave them a ladder, not only a hammer — but know that some will climb their pride instead. Their resting place is named so that you do not envy their temporary win in the argument.

207:
"And of the people is he who sells himself, seeking means to the approval of Allah. And Allah is kind to the servants."

Opposite portrait. A person who sells himself — gives his whole person, life, preference, safety — seeking ridwan Allah, His pleasure. Not selling religion for a small price as earlier verses condemned, but selling the self to buy nearness. Companions like Suhayb, who left his wealth to emigrate, were remembered under this spirit; others who threw themselves into battle seeking Allah's face likewise.

Allah is ra'uf with the servants — tender-kind. He does not waste such a sale. The Prophet, peace be upon him, said that whoever seeks Allah's pleasure at the cost of people's anger, Allah will be enough for him against people. The kindness of Allah toward those who offer themselves is the quiet engine of every sacrifice that looks irrational on a spreadsheet.

You may not be asked for a single dramatic sale. You are asked daily: a portion of sleep, pride, money, plan. Sell something of yourself for His pleasure and trust the Ra'uf who named Himself at the end of the bargain.

208:
"O you who believe, enter into Islam completely and do not follow the footsteps of Satan. Indeed, he is to you a clear enemy."

Enter into silm — Islam, peace, the whole of submission — kafah, completely. Not one foot in the Book and one foot in a life that ignores it. Partial religion was a temptation in Madinah: take the easy rites, leave the costly ones; keep the identity, drop the ethics. The verse refuses a buffet Islam.

Do not follow Satan's footsteps — again the gradual tracks. He loves partial entry because the unentered room becomes his office. The Prophet, peace be upon him, said the believer is like a horse tied by its tether, and he taught that when you leave a gap in practice the shaytan finds a bed. He also said this religion is solid; enter it gently but aim for the whole, not for burn-out theatre followed by collapse.

Complete entry is a direction more than a claim of perfection overnight. Keep walking into the parts you still avoid — money, tongue, family rights, prayer on time — and refuse the enemy who always suggests a smaller Islam would be more sophisticated.

209:
"But if you slip after clear proofs have come to you, then know that Allah is Almighty and Wise."

Clear proofs remove the excuse of ignorance. If after that you zallaltum — slip, slide — know who you are dealing with: Aziz, invincible in consequence; Hakim, wise in how He deals with the slip. The pairing prevents two mistakes: thinking you can outrun His power, and thinking His response is chaotic revenge without wisdom.

Slips after clarity still happen; tawbah still works. The Prophet, peace be upon him, said all of the children of Adam err and the best of those who err are those who repent. He also said the one who repents from sin is like one with no sin. Knowing He is Aziz and Hakim should accelerate return, not freeze the sinner in despair. Power means the sin mattered; wisdom means the door He opens back is real and well-placed.

When you fall after knowledge, do not add the stupidity of pretending the proofs were unclear. Name the slip, return, repair what you can, and let Almighty and Wise handle both justice and mercy better than your panic will. The verse is a warning to the stubborn and a map for the fallen who still want home.

210:
"Do they await but that Allah should come to them in covers of clouds and the angels as well, and the matter is then decided? And to Allah all matters are returned."

Some delay faith as if waiting for a cinematic unveiling — God and angels arriving in canopies of cloud — after which decision is forced and choice expires. The verse says, in effect: if you are waiting for that, understand that when it comes the exam is over. The matter is qudiya — settled. Returns are to Allah either way.

The Quran repeatedly warns that demanding the final sign is demanding the end of free response (6:158). The Prophet, peace be upon him, described the sun rising from the west as a gate of tawbah closing, and he said Allah accepts the servant's repentance until the death rattle. Waiting for compulsion is not caution; it is gambling the only window in which belief is chosen rather than extracted by terror of the obvious.

Believe while belief still counts as trust in the unseen. The clouds of the final scene are not a better opportunity. They are the end of opportunity. Return your matter to Allah now, in willing surrender, before every matter is returned to Him without your consultation.

211:
"Ask the Children of Israel how many a clear sign We gave them. And whoever exchanges the favour of Allah after it has come to him — then indeed, Allah is severe in penalty."

The question is historical and present. How many clear signs were given to the Children of Israel — sea, manna, prophets, scripture — is a known story in this surah already. The principle: whoever changes Allah's ni'mah after it arrives, trading it for denial or distortion, meets severity of punishment. Favour is an amanah. Receiving more proof raises the cost of refusal.

The Prophet, peace be upon him, feared for his ummah not poverty but the world opening upon them as it opened on those before, and he told the story of nations destroyed after blessings were met with arrogance. Severity is not the first attribute named in the Quran, but it is real for those who convert gifts into arguments against the Giver.

Inventory your own signs — guidance you did not deserve, knowledge you were taught, safety you walk in — and do not be the person who uses them as furniture while refusing the One who sent them.

212:
"Beautified for those who disbelieve is the life of this world, and they ridicule those who believe. But those who fear Allah will be above them on the Day of Resurrection. And Allah gives provision to whom He wills without account."

The world is made zuyyina — adorned — in the eyes of those who disbelieve. That adornment explains their mockery of believers who restrain themselves for an unseen future. Laughter at hijab, at refused interest, at prayer that interrupts the meeting — all of it sits in this psychology. What is sparkled looks like the only real thing.

On the Day, those who had taqwa are above them. The seating chart flips. Provision without account is Allah's to give in both abodes; He is not bound to the mockers' metrics of success. The Prophet, peace be upon him, said the world is a prison for the believer and a paradise for the disbeliever — not because the believer never smiles, but because his limits are real and the disbeliever's feast has no after-bill in his imagination.

When mockery stings, read the end of the verse. Above them. Provision without account. The adornment was a test of vision. Close your eyes, then open them on the scale that Day uses.

Leave the labels that make riba sound clever — 'growth product,' 'convenience fee,' 'time value' dressed to hide excess. The Quran already knew the arguments and still drew the line. Your task is exit with tawbah and principal, not a better brand name for the same war.
213:
"Mankind was one community; then Allah sent the prophets as bringers of good tidings and warners and sent down with them the Scripture in truth to judge among the people concerning that in which they differed. And none differed over the Scripture except those who were given it — after the clear proofs came to them — out of jealous animosity among themselves. And Allah guided those who believed to the truth concerning that over which they had differed, by His permission. And Allah guides whom He wills to a straight path."

Humanity began on shared fitrah; difference that needed revelation grew as time and desire pulled communities apart. Prophets came bashir and nadhir, with Book in truth to judge the disputes. The tragedy named: the deepest splits over the Book came from people who had it, after proofs, because of baghy — envious rivalry between them. Knowledge did not kill envy; envy used knowledge as a weapon.

Allah guided the believers to the truth in what was disputed, by His permission. Guidance is not always with the largest sect of the old dispute; it is with those who surrender to what He clarifies. The Prophet, peace be upon him, came as that clarification for what People of the Book disputed, and he warned his ummah against repeating baghy under new names.

When scholars or groups fight with scriptures as clubs, suspect baghy before you suspect the text. Ask for the path that looks like permission of Allah — sincerity, humility, unity on the clear — not the path that only enlarges a camp.

Ethics in conflict are part of faith, not decoration after victory. The same Book that allows force fences it. If your anger cannot accept a fence, it is not yet fighting in the way of Allah.
214:
"Or do you think that you will enter Paradise while such trial has not yet come to you as came to those who passed on before you? They were touched by poverty and hardship and were shaken until the Messenger and those who believed with him said, 'When is the help of Allah?' Unquestionably, the help of Allah is near."

A hard verse for a young ummah and for every later reader who wants Paradise on ease. Did you think you would enter without facing the like of what earlier believers faced? Poverty, harm, and zalzalah — shaking that rattles the soul — until even the Messenger and those with him cried, "When is Allah's help?" That cry is not disbelief; it is human strain recorded with honesty. The answer lands immediately: surely Allah's help is near.

The Prophet, peace be upon him, and his companions lived this at the trench, at Uhud, in the boycott years. He said the most tried people are the prophets, then the likeliest, then the likeliest. He also said the help of Allah comes according to the need, and with hardship goes ease (94:5-6).

If you are shaken, you are not thereby abandoned. You may even be on the prophetic pattern. Say with them, "When is the help?" as longing, not as denial — and believe the end of the ayah: it is near.

215:
"They ask you what they should spend. Say, 'Whatever you spend of good is for parents and relatives and orphans and the needy and the traveller. And whatever you do of good — indeed, Allah knows of it.'"

The question is about what/to whom to spend. The answer lists people first, not percentages: parents, relatives, orphans, needy, traveller. Charity starts near and circles out — the same moral geometry as 2:83 and 2:177. "Whatever you do of good, Allah knows it" means the unadvertised transfer, the quiet support of a parent, is already on record.

The Prophet, peace be upon him, said begin with those you support, and that the upper hand is better than the lower, and that a coin spent on a family is a greater charity than a coin spent far away in some cases of duty. He also said Allah is shy to turn away empty the hands raised to Him — knowledge of good is not cold accounting; it is care.

When you ask where your money should go, start with the names this verse starts with. Then expand. And stop worrying that unseen good is wasted. He knows it.

216:
"Fighting has been ordained for you while it is hateful to you. But perhaps you hate a thing and it is good for you; and perhaps you love a thing and it is bad for you. And Allah knows, while you know not."

Combat was written upon the Madinan community after years of restraint, and they disliked it — as normal humans dislike risk and blood. The verse does not shame the dislike; it reframes knowledge. You may hate what is good for you and love what is bad for you. Allah knows; you do not know fully.

This principle outgrows its occasion. Medicine that tastes bitter, a breakup that saves the din, a job refusal that protects salah, a battle that removes persecution — the pattern repeats. The Prophet, peace be upon him, sought counsel, prepared, and still taught that outcomes are with Allah. He said wonderful is the affair of the believer: all of it is good — if ease, gratitude; if harm, patience.

When your preference screams, leave a margin for this ayah. Hate is not a reliable fatwa. Love is not a reliable fatwa. Ask what Allah knows, through His law and through trusted counsel, and walk with the humility of "you know not."

Ethics in conflict are part of faith, not decoration after victory. The same Book that allows force fences it. If your anger cannot accept a fence, it is not yet fighting in the way of Allah.
217:
"They ask you about fighting in the sacred month. Say, 'Fighting therein is a great sin, but averting people from the way of Allah, and disbelief in Him, and the Sacred Mosque, and expelling its people from it are greater with Allah. And fitnah is greater than killing.' And they will continue to fight you until they turn you back from your religion if they are able. And whoever of you reverts from his religion and dies while he is a disbeliever — for those, their deeds have become worthless in this world and the Hereafter, and those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein eternally."

A raid in a sacred month became a propaganda stick against Muslims. The Quran admits fighting in that month is kabir — major — then places greater crimes on the scale: blocking Allah's path, disbelief, barring the Sacred Mosque, expelling its people. Fitnah, persecution to pry people from faith, is worse than the killing the Quraysh suddenly claimed to abhor. They will keep fighting you until they make you apostates if they can — a clear read of enemy war aims in that moment.

Apostasy under pressure ending in death upon disbelief voids deeds and ends in the Fire forever. The severity matches the campaign: this was not casual theology; it was a war on faith's continuity. The Prophet, peace be upon him, lived the sequel with treaties and battles until Makkah opened and expulsion was reversed.

Read the proportions carefully. Sacred time matters. Persecution and forced deconversion matter more. And the believer is warned that the other side's project may be your religious ruin, not only your military defeat — so guard the heart as carefully as the border.
218:
"Indeed, those who have believed and those who have emigrated and fought in the cause of Allah — those expect the mercy of Allah. And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful."

After the stern warning about apostasy, the surah praises those who stacked the opposite choices: faith, hijrah, and jihad in Allah's path. They yarjun — hope for, expect — Allah's mercy. Hope here is not wishful fog; it is expectation built on promises from the Truthful.

Forgiving and Merciful closes so that even this elite path is framed by mercy, not by self-earned immunity. The Prophet, peace be upon him, said there is no hijrah after the conquest of Makkah in the old sense but jihad and intention continue, and he taught that deeds are by intentions. Emigration today may be leaving a sin, a toxic place, a haram income for Allah's sake — still a departure toward Him.

Stack what you can of the three: deepen iman, emigrate from what He hates, struggle where He commands. Then expect mercy — not because you are flawless, but because He named Himself Forgiving and Merciful over people who try.

219:
"They ask you about wine and gambling. Say, 'In them is great sin and benefits for people, but their sin is greater than their benefit.' And they ask you what they should spend. Say, 'The excess.' Thus Allah makes clear to you the verses that you might give thought —"

A staged answer in the journey to full prohibition. Khamr and maysir have ithm kabir and also some manafi' — trade, temporary thrill, social oil. The criterion is not "does it have any benefit?" but which side is greater. Sin outweighs. Later verses will seal total avoidance (5:90); here the moral math is taught so the ummah learns how to weigh.

They also ask what to spend: al-'afw — the surplus beyond need. Not the amount that destroys your dependents, not the hoard that never feels enough to give from. The Prophet, peace be upon him, said the best charity is what leaves wealth enough, and begin with your dependents. He also said every intoxicant is khamr and every khamr is haram, completing the arc this verse begins.

Think — la'allakum tatafakkarun. Islam trains weighing harms and benefits under revelation's scale, not under appetite's scale. Where sin is greater, the smart heart does not bargain forever for the smaller benefit.

220:
"— upon this world and the Hereafter. And they ask you about orphans. Say, 'Improvement for them is best. And if you mix your affairs with theirs — they are your brothers. And Allah knows the corrupter from the reformer. And if Allah had willed, He could have put you in difficulty. Indeed, Allah is Almighty and Wise.'"

Thought about wine and spending was to stretch across dunya and akhirah together. Then orphans: the fear of mismixing funds after strict warnings had made some companions isolate orphans' food uncomfortably. The answer: islah — betterment — is the best policy. If you mix living arrangements, they are your brothers. Allah knows who ruins and who repairs. He could have made the rules crushing; He did not. Aziz and Hakim again — power that could burden, wisdom that chose manageable duty.

The Prophet, peace be upon him, said he and the sponsor of an orphan are like these two fingers in Paradise, and he warned that the one who devours orphan wealth ingests fire. Brotherhood language kills the cold "ward versus guardian" abuse pattern.

Seek the orphan's islah in money, schooling, and tenderness. Mix without stealing. God knows the difference, and He made the path walkable on purpose.
